Genomic characterization of recombinant cucumber mosaic virus isolates infecting mustard species via HTS in India
Pankhuri Singhal’ | Malyaj R. Prajapati? | Damini Diksha’ Virendra Kumar Baranwal'® | Jitender Singh?
‘Division of Plant Pathology, ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi, India
College of Biotechnology, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel University of Agriculture and Technology, Meerut, India
Correspondence
Virendra Kumar Baranwal, Division of Plant Pathology, ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi 110012, India. Email: vbaranwal2001@yahoo.com
Abstract
One of the most pervasive plant viruses, the cucumber mosaic virus (CMV),

Bromoviridae: Cucumovirus, infects a variety of plants worldwide and significantly af- fects production quality and quantity. Viral infection exhibiting severe mosaic and stunting symptoms in plants infected with turnip mosaic virus was observed in ex- perimental fields in IARI. Leaf samples were collected and the virome was identified through high-throughput sequencing subjecting ribosomal RNA-depleted mRNA. Here, we unravel for the first time the complete genome sequences of two CMV iso- lates infecting yellow and black-seeded mustard in India. The three segments of the viral genome, as well as coat protein cds, were amplified and subjected to Sanger se- quencing. The three viral genomic components were 3348 of RNA1, 3032 and 3040 of RNA2, 2260 and 2236nts of RNA 3, respectively (including the 5’ and 3’ UTR). The two isolates shared high sequence identity and clubbed with the subgroup-IB isolates in a clade. Recombination signals were detected within all the three RNAs of both New Delhi isolates wherein one of the parent isolates was reported to infect the family Brassicaceae. Recombination was observed throughout the region of RNA2 but the 3’ UTR was observed to be most prone to recombination. This is the first com- prehensive depiction of a recombinant CMV subgroup IB isolate from black, yellow and brown-seeded mustard from India, which has implications for its robust detection and overall management. This study also provides insight into population structuring, host expansions, level of genetic heterogeneity and variability of worldwide prevalent CMV isolates.
KEYWORDS
black mustard, cucumber mosaic virus, complete genome sequence, genetic diversity, subgroups, yellow mustard, brown mustard
1 | INTRODUCTION

Mustard belonging to the family Brassicaceae is not only an es- sential source of edible oil in India but also a condiment and vegetable leaf source. After soybean, mustard is India's second most significant oilseed crop. There are three major varieties of

mustard: yellow mustard (Brassica rapa subsp. trilocularis), thought to have Mediterranean origin; brown mustard, sometimes known as Indian mustard (Brassica juncea); and black mustard (B. nigra), thought to have Asia Minor-lran origin. Several viruses have been found to infect mustard in India, including turnip yellows virus (TuYV) (Sharma et al., 2013), turnip mosaic virus (TUMV)

(Singhal et al., 2022), croton yellow vein mosaic virus (CY VMV) (Roy et al., 2013).

The viruses that have recently “jumped host species” cause the worst virus infections (Villarreal et al., 2000). The identification of plant viruses and their mixed infections has increased significantly due to high-throughput sequencing coupled with bioinformatics analysis (Nabi et al., 2022; Prajapati et al., 2022; Singhal et al., 2021, 2022; Villamor et al., 2019). The purpose of this study was to exam- ine the viral spectrum of this essential oilseed plant. On observation of symptoms of severe mosaic, puckering and stunting in mustard experimental fields of Indian Council of Agricultural Research-Indian Agricultural Research Institute (ICAR-IARI), New Delhi, the associ- ation of viruses was hypothesized for which leaf sample collection was done and sent for virome analysis via high-throughput RNAseq approach. Our study indicated invariable association of turnip mo- saic virus (TuMV) with the diseased mustard plant but association of cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) was also observed along with TUMV by electron microscopy and reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR; Singhal et al., 2022). Several CMV isolates are known to cause symptoms ranging from minor mosaic to severe stunting and necrosis (Lee et al., 2007). CMV necrotic pathotypes have previously been identified in tomato and tobacco (Divéki et al., 2004; Jorda, 1992). We confirmed the infection of CMV in all mustard species via electron microscopy and RT-PCR.

CMV, a member of the Cucumovirus genus under the family Bromoviridae ranks one in the order of importance of plant viruses, probably due to its worldwide distribution, broadest host range infecting more than a thousand plant species and fast expanding host range (Jacquemond, 2012). It is known to cause a wide range of specific symptoms in hosts such as foliar mosaic, shoestring/fern leaf, yellowing, systemic necrosis, blight, ringspot, stunting, infec- tious chlorosis, heart rot and dwarfing (Jacquemond, 2012; Zitter & Murphy, 2009). It is transmitted by seed, mechanical inoculation and by more than 60 aphid species in a non-persistent manner (Palukaitis & Garcia-Arenal, 2003).

Cucumber mosaic virus is an icosahedral/isometric particle with an approximately 28-30nm diameter with a tripartite genome of single-stranded positive-sense RNAs (RNA 1, 2, 3) of about 8700 nucleotides (nt) encompassing five open reading frames (ORFs) (Palukaitis & Garcia-Arenal, 2003). ORF 1a and 2a encode replica- tion components, whereas ORF 2b encodes a viral RNA silencing suppressor implicated in virus mobility and pathogenicity. ORF 3a and 3b contain the movement protein (MP) and the coat protein (CP), respectively (Canto et al., 1997). Isolates of CMV are categorized into subgroups (I and II) based on the sequence identity, CP peptide mapping, serology, nucleic acid hybridization and RT-PCR RFLP of amplicons (Palukaitis et al., 1992; Roossinck, 2002). Based on the CP gene and the 5’ non-translated region (5’ UTR) of RNA 3, subgroup lis further divided into IA and IB (Roossinck, 2002). In this study, we used high-throughput sequencing and subsequent validation by sanger sequencing to examine and characterize the entire genome sequences of two CMV isolates infecting yellow and black-seeded mustard.

| MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1 | Collection of virus samples and electron microscopic studies

In January 2021, viral disease symptoms were observed in the ex- perimental mustard field of ICAR-IARI, New Delhi. Leaf samples from brown, black and yellow-seeded mustard varieties exhibiting suspected symptoms of viral diseases were collected. The field- collected symptomatic leaf samples were examined under an elec- tron microscope (EM) using the leaf dip technique in 2% aqueous uranyl acetate (UA).
2.2 | High-throughput RNAseq, sequence processing and assembly

The total RNA was extracted from leaf samples of black-seeded (New Delhi BM) and yellow-seeded mustard (New Delhi YM) culti- vars via the Qiagen RNeasy plant micro kit. The quality and quantity of total RNA were analysed using the QubitTM fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and TapeStation (Agilent). The Ribo-Zero rRNA removal kit was used to remove ribosomal RNA from total RNA (Illumina). Libraries were produced using the truseq-stranded-total RNA library preparation kit in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions (Illumina). The Bioanalyzer (Agilent) and TapeStation (Agilent) were used to validate the sequence library. The Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform was used for the HTS.

Following sequencing, FastP v.0.20.0 was used to remove adapt- ers, poly-N sequences (15%), and low-quality reads. CLC Genomic workbench was used to assemble the trimmed HTS reads of sam- ples. Homology analysis was performed on assembled contig data- sets using NCBI Btastn and BLAstx against the NCBI viral genome and protein databases.
2.3. | Sequence validation through polymerase chain reaction and sequencing

The High-throughput RNAseq led to the construction of CMV ge- nomes which were verified using a two-step RT-PCR. The CiustaLW multiple sequence alignment software, integrated with BioEpit v.7.2.3, was used to align the viral sequences assembled via Illumina. A consensus sequence obtained was used to design PCR prim- ers for RNA1 (Forward-5’ CAAGAGCGTACGGTTCAATCCC-3’ and Reverse-3’ TTGGAGGCCCCCACAAAGTG-5’); RNA2 (Forward-5’ CAAGAGCGTACGGTTCAATCCC-3’ and Reverse-3’ AGTGGGGG GTACCCGTA-5’) and RNA3 (Forward-5’ GTGTGTGTGTGTGT CGCGT-3’ and Reverse-3’ AGTGGGGGGTACCCGTA-5’) segments of CMV along with CP region of RNA3 (Forward-5' GGATCCATGGA CAAATCTGAATCA-3’ and Reverse-3' GAGCTCTCAAACTGGGA GCAC-5’) manually. With slight modification to the manufacturer's methodology, the first strand of complementary DNA (cDNA) was

synthesized using the FIREScript® RT cDNA synthesis kit. It was am- plified using standard PCR consisting of an initial denaturation step at 94°C for 2min, 35cycles of denaturation at 94°C for 45s, anneal- ing at 65°C for RNA1 for 3.5 min/66°C for RNA2 for 3.5min/60°C for RNA for 2.5 min followed by final primer extension at 72°C for 10min. The PCR mixture consisted of 500ng of cDNA template, 12.5 ,1L GoTaq® Long PCR master mix (Promega) and 1p1L each of forward and reverse primer in a total volume of 25 pL.

For the amplification of the CP region of RNA3 from 10 samples, the standard PCR cycle consisted of an initial denaturation step at 94°C for 4min, 35cycles of denaturation at 94°C for 45s, anneal- ing at 58°C for CP for 1min and extension at 72°C for 1 min, fol- lowed by final primer extension at 72°C for 10min. The PCR mixture consisted of 500ng of cDNA template, 12.5. DreamTaq™ green PCR master mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific®) and 1,1L each of for- ward and reverse primer in a total volume of 25,1L. PCR-generated amplicons were separated on 1% agarose gel (1X TAE containing 0.01% ethidium bromide electrophoretically and visualized in a gel documentation system; BIO-RAD). According to the manufacturer's instructions, the particular DNA amplified fragments were purified using the GeneJET PCR purification kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific®) and cloned into the pGEM-T easy vector (Promega). The cloned seg- ments were sequenced. BLASTN 2.9.0+ was used to confirm consen- sus sequences, and comparisons were made with the whole CMV sequences compiled from Illumina reads.
2.4 | Sequence, phylogenetic, diversity and selection pressure analyses

The whole genome sequences of 32 CMV isolates of RNA1 and RNA2 and 36 isolates of RNA3 retrieved from GenBank and the two isolates identified in this study, were submitted to phylogenetic anal- ysis and sequence identity and genetic distance estimation to assess the evolutionary connections among the CMV isolates. Utilizing MEGA version XI's Ciusta.W (Thompson et al., 1994), multiple sequence alignments were carried out (Tamura et al., 2021). The phylogenetic trees were built using the maximum-likelihood method with 1000 bootstrapping to assess the validity of the branches, with the pea- nut stunt virus (PSV) reference sequence used as an outgroup. The compositions of the nucleotide and amino acid sequences, as well as the percentage of sequence identity, were calculated using BioEbit 7.2 (Hall, 1999). Genetic distances were calculated in meca version XI using the best-fitting nucleotide substitution model Tamura-Nei (p-distances based on nucleotide or amino acid identity).

Based on several permutation statistical tests (Ky, Kp Z, San and Fey), the DnaSP software application version 6.10.01 with de- fault settings (Rozas et al. 2017) was used to assess the gene flow and genetic differentiation among the CMV isolates population (Hudson, 2000). The statistical tests based on permutation sup- ported by ap value less than 0.05 were used. The Non-synonymous (dN) and synonymous (dS) differences were statistically evaluated at the individual codon level in the polyprotein by the SLAC and FUBAR methods to establish the type of selection pressure on the

2.5 | Recombination analyses

In this study, we sought to characterize recombination events in 32 full genome sequences of CMV isolates from different parts of the world including the two New Delhi isolates using RDP4. For RNA 3, 36 sequences were analysed. RDP, GENECONv (Sawyer, 1999), BOOTSCAN (Salminen et al., 1995), cHimeara (Posada & Crandall, 2001), Maxcui (Smith, 1992), siscan (Gibbs et al., 2000), and 3Seq were used in con- junction in the rpp version 4 software package to identify potential recombination events in the sequences (Martin et al., 2015). All of the isolates that the rpp version 4 algorithms identified as potential recombinants were taken into account, and their major and minor parents as well as recombination breakpoints were identified.
3 | RESULTS
3.1. | Symptomatology, EM analysis and RT-PCR

The symptoms of stunting (Figure 1a,b), puckering and severe mo- saic (Figure 1c) were observed in the experimental mustard fields at IARI, New Delhi. The leaf samples from various yellow-seeded mus- tard (Pusa Gold), black-seeded mustard (BN-3), brown-seeded con- ventional (Pusa Vijay) and quality mustard (single zero type [PM-30 and Pusa Karishma] and double zero type [JC-21, JC-33 and PDZ1, PDZ-5, PDZM-33]) varieties were analysed in this study. EM analy- sis revealed the presence of flexuous particles (Singhal et al., 2022), but the presence of spherical particles indicated mixed infection of viruses as well (Figure S1).
3.2 | Determination of the complete genome sequence of CMV isolates using RNAseq high throughput sequencing approaches

The HTS of pooled symptomatic leaf samples of black-seeded mus- tard (BM) and yellow-seeded mustard (YM) varieties were performed by applying the ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-depleted approach. High- throughput Illumina libraries of 123,561,190 and 108,345,808 bp total reads from BM and YM, respectively, were used to construct CMV genomes (Table 1) which were subjected to quality trimming and 37,701 and 51,819 contigs were constructed from BM and YM leaves, respectively. A BLasTN search against the nt database was performed on all contigs, revealing the existence of CMV whole- genome sequences. Sequence assembly using reference-based map- ping and de novo assembly produced consistent findings. Both black and yellow seeded mustard contained CMV, with read counts of 15,318 (0.012%) and 318,701 (0.294%), respectively. This indicates a high viral titre of CMV in the yellow-seeded mustard.

3.3. | Wet-lab validation of CMV in mustard genotypes in field and containment facility

The PCR amplicons of approximately 3328, 3015 and 2158 bp, were ob- tained in the tested samples for RNA1, RNA2 and RNA3, respectively, whereas negative control showed no amplification during RT-PCR. The amplified sequences were submitted to NCBI. Further, eight to ten pooled plants of each variety were tested for the presence of CMV in three replicates using CP-specific primer. Positive amplification was ob- tained, indicating the presence of CMV in all the varieties of three spe- cies of mustard. The amplified sequences with CP primer of 657 bp from six samples were submitted in NCBI and were found to share around 98.93% sequence similarity with complete cds of CP (AY125575).

The genome of RNA2 and RNA3 of YM and BM had an addition of 6 and 24 nts at 3’ UTR. While the size and position of 5’ UTR and all other ORFs were similar in both isolates (Table 2). Based on whole genome comparative recombination analysis of the CMV isolates, 28 potential breakpoints were detected, with RNA1 ranked first (RNA1>RNA2=RNA3). Among all CMV isolates con- sidered, 10 recombination sites were found in RNA1 with a recom- bination frequency of 28. In RNA2, both UTRs and two ORFs are prone to recombination, with nine hotspots and a recombination frequency of 23. While in RNA3, though, nine recombination sites were found but only at a frequency of 14.

In most cases, similar recombination events were noticed for CMV BM and YM (Table 4). CMV New Delhi isolates showed very close evolutionary ties to India's clove basil isolate and Japan's brown mustard, acting as major and minor parents, respectively, in RNA1. The recombinant site was observed to be 3’ NTR. In total, out of 32, 22 (68.75%) isolates were observed to be recombinants. Most isolates were recombinants of vir capsicum from Italy and New Delhi, tomato from India, belonging to subgroup Ib.

3.7 | Population dynamics and selection pressure

The degree of differentiation and gene flow was measured in whole genome sequences of all three RNAs of different CMV subgroups (Table 5). The subgroup la with II was found to have the lowest K., followed by la with Ib, and the highest K, were found between Ib and II for all three RNAs. Further, the lowest K, values were observed for RNAS for all three subgroups. The results of genetic differentiation are confirmed by the opposite values of K,, to K,. For undifferenti- ated and fully differentiated populations, respectively, the value of F., ranged from 0 to 1. Infrequent gene flow is seen as having oc- curred if |F,;|>0.33 or |N,,|1. In all the subgroups, the F,, was found to be above 0.33 for all three RNA sequences. The values of F,; were higher between lb and II (above 0.86) and lowest between Ib and la (around 0.4) in all three RNAs.

Patterns of selection imposed on the genomic segments of CMV were subsequently investigated to compare the level of selection among coding areas via the ratios of dN/dS per coding site. Across all the CMV segments, the mean (dN/dS) values were obtained from pairwise comparisons between sequences, indicating the occur- rence of purifying or negative selection. The CP gene was found to have the highest value, followed by the 2b gene, while the 1a and 2a genes had the lowest value. The selection pressure value was found to be greater (Table 6). 4 | DISCUSSION

Since prospective hosts are more frequently present in the environ- ment, generalist viruses with broad host ranges such as CMV can be particularly destructive. A molecular population genetic framework was utilized to analyse the evolution and host extension of CMV, a highly pathogenic plant RNA virus, using the sequence data of the en- tire genome of RNA segments. Historically, CMV was first described

Here, we report the host shift of CMV to infect black and yellow- seeded mustard in India. The plants exhibiting severe mosaic, puck- ering and stunting were found to be infected by both CMV and TuMV while the samples exhibiting puckering symptoms were in- fected with only TuMV (Singhal et al., 2022). The genomic sequences of two CMV isolates i.e., CMV YM and CMV BM- in this investigation shared their highest levels of identity with isolates from South-East Asian nations that belong to the subgroup IB (India, Taiwan, China and Italy). Other CMV isolates belonging to subgroups IA and II
SINGHAL er at.

have also been reported from India (Koundal et al., 2011). The New Delhi isolates' grouping in subgroup IB has been confirmed based on the highest sequence similarity of the 5’ UTR of RNA as well as sequence similarity in RNA1, 2, and 3 with the isolates belong- ing to subgroup IB from Taiwan, Italy, and India (Raj et al., 2017; Roossinck, 2002). Phylogeny estimations for the Cucumovirus genus with New Delhi isolates revealed that the trees for each RNA were noncongruent, indicating that the evolutionary histories of the RNAs were independent of each other, as already reported (White et al., 1995). This strongly supports a model of reassortment as a mechanism for isolate generation and speciation.

The similarity values (Table S1) and genetic distance values (Table 3) of CMV New Delhi isolates for all three RNAs were con- sistent with the earlier recorded estimates viz., 92%-94% (IA/IB), 74%-78% (IA/II) and 73%-78% (|B/Il) (Roossinck, 2001). The genetic distance analysis indicates the most significant evolutionary diver- gence of sequence pairs within the subgroup IB followed by IA and II. Subgroups IA and II are present all across the world, but subgroup IB is primarily found in Asia (Palukaitis & Garcia-Arenal, 2003). Within subgroup-IB, RNA1 sequence pairs were under major divergent force while RNA3 were under least divergence. The mean genetic distance observations were as per the phylogenetic tree generated via the maximum likelihood method for the sub-grouping of CMV isolates.

RNA recombination facilitates plant virus diversity and adapt- ability to new hosts, and it commonly produces novel variants and viral isolates that overcome resistance. The RNA 2 of New Delhi isolates were intralineage of subgroup IB, while RNA 1 were inter- lineage recombinants of IA and IB. But in the case of RNA3, inter and intralineage recombination was observed. Our findings also indicated that the Asian isolates (India, China and Japan) played a substantial role in the genome reconstruction of CMV. Among the three RNAs, RNA1 was the most prone to recombination. In gen- eral, intralineage recombinations (within subgroups IA and IB) were more likely than interlineage ones. One of the recombinant parent for CMV New Delhi isolates in the case of all three RNAs was re- ported to infect a member family Brassicaceae indicating its role in adaption to mustard as a new host. The isolates exhibiting reassort- ments between the two subgroups will be more likely to adapt to new host plants than parental viruses. They play an essential part in the evolution and survival of New Delhi isolates in new hosts. The 3’ NTR of all three RNAs was the most recombination-prone region in New Delhi isolates. Similar to this study, recombinations in the ORF regions have been quite rare as compared to the non-coding regions which have been found to be more prone to recombination (Bonnet et al., 2005; Jacquemond, 2012). While in other studies, the RNA2 region that overlaps ORFs (2a/2b) is reported to be the most susceptible to recombination, indicating that regulatory components are present in this region that control the differential expression of 2a and 2b (Koundal et al., 2011).

The natural selection data analysis revealed that all CMV ge- nomic regions were under the dominant control of negative (or purifying) selection. Prior research has also demonstrated that CMV encoded proteins are subject to this form of selection (Liu
9 ipa WILEY

et al., 2009; Moury, 2004). High dN/dS values for CP and 2b gene indicate that these two genes have a higher tolerance for amino acid changes tending toward its less variable nature. The 2b gene might be a driving factor for host dependency and adaptability. All other genes underwent varied degrees of purifying to the neutral selection, which attributes to preserving the protein functions and reducing the frequency of less fit virus variants. In other reports, the 1a, MP and CP genes showed low (dN/dS) ratios, suggesting high selective pressure (Nouri et al., 2014). The few sites of CMV that underwent positive selection might be due to CMV adjust- ing to new hosts as the positive selections endow the virus with more fitness to adapt to a new host as well as environment (Kim et al., 2014).

Taking all the value trends under consideration, a high genetic differentiation was observed between isolates of IA with II, followed by IB with II and the least between IA and IB. The high F,, values and low N,, values between IB and II indicate extremely low gene flow, while gene flow was observed to be highest between IA and IB. The above analysis suggests the coevolving nature of isolates belonging to subgroups IA and IB.

This work reports two new recombinant CMV isolates from India infecting new hosts i.e., yellow and black-seeded mustard for the first time. Also, the CMV CP was amplified from brown mustard as a host from India for the first time. The probabilistic host expan- sion could be due to the host jump via vectors (aphids) in winter. Studies on genetic distance, diversity, and variability revealed that the segment RNA3 gene, followed by RNA2, is highly conserved, while RNA1 was the most variable. The observation of 2a and 2b subgroups exhibiting positive selection sites and recombination might be the consequence of the adaptation of CMV to novel hosts. Our findings contributed to our understanding of CMV's evolution, host expansion and genetic conservation in India. The CMV's patho- genic mechanism and cruciferous crops' resistance will be important research topics in the future.
